## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Parantapajātaka* (Ja 416) is a narrative belonging to the *Sattanipāta* (Book of Sevens) in the second chapter, the *Gandharavagga*, of the canonical Pali *Jātaka* collection [Fausböll 1883]. The framing story is set at the Bamboo Grove (Veḷuvana), where the Buddha addresses the assembly regarding Devadatta’s persistent efforts to kill him by hiring archers, hurling a boulder, and dispatching the rogue elephant Nāḷāgiri [SuttaCentral]. The Buddha relates that in a previous existence as well, Devadatta attempted to destroy him, gaining nothing but distress in return [SuttaCentral]. The canonical verse portion opens with the incipit *Āgamissati me pāpaṁ* [Fausböll 1883].

In the tale of the past, a monarch flees his besieged city at night in disguise accompanied by his pregnant chief queen, his family priest (purohita), and an attendant named Parantapa, establishing a hermitage in the forest [Cowell 1897]. While the king and priest forage for wild fruits, Parantapa commits adultery with the queen [Cowell 1897]. Fearing disclosure once the child is born, the queen conspires with Parantapa to ambush and assassinate the king at his bathing place on the river bank, where Parantapa beheads and buries him—a murder witnessed from an overhanging tree by the concealed priest [Cowell 1897]. At the conclusion (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies the characters of the past life, revealing that the slain king was Devadatta and the royal prince was the Bodhisatta [Fausböll 1883].

No cross-language parallels in Sanskrit, Chinese, or Tibetan are identified for this text [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus detects nine internal Pali text-reuse segments between the verse text and the third volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, the longest running from §5.1 to §7.1 [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records four translations of the jātaka across four modern languages [SuttaCentral].
